title: Aglianico
description: Southern Italy's great red: late-ripening, tannic and acidic, grown on volcanic hills in Campania and Basilicata.
L: Aglianico gives deep-coloured wines with high tannin and high acidity, a rare combination in a southern grape. Aromas include black cherry, plum, leather, tar, smoke and dried herbs. Its power and ageing potential have earned it the nickname the Barolo of the south.

Aglianico has grown in southern Italy for centuries. Its name was once linked to Hellenic, suggesting a Greek origin, but DNA hasn't confirmed this, and the name may come from a Spanish-era word. It ripens very late, often in November, which lets it keep acidity even in a warm region.
Why does Aglianico keep high acidity in the warm south of Italy?
It ripens very late, in cooler autumn weather, often at altitude
Late ripening at altitude, into cool autumn nights, preserves acidity.

In the glass, Aglianico is dark ruby. On the nose, black cherry, plum, smoke and earth. On the palate, firm, sometimes rustic tannins, bright acidity and a long finish. Young wines can be severe; age brings leather, tobacco and dried fruit.
Which aromas are typical of Aglianico?
Aglianico combines high tannin and high acidity
It ripens very late, keeping freshness in the south
It's called the Barolo of the south for its power and age
Explain the role of volcanic soils

Aglianico grows mainly in Campania, around Naples and inland in Irpinia, and in Basilicata, on the slopes of Monte Vulture. Smaller amounts grow in Puglia and Molise. There are some plantings in Australia and California, but it remains overwhelmingly Italian.

Both key areas are volcanic: Irpinia has volcanic ash over clay and limestone; Vulture is an extinct volcano. Volcanic soils drain well and give a smoky, mineral edge. Altitude, often 400 to 700 m, gives cool nights. Together they explain how a late grape ripens slowly and keeps freshness.
Monte Vulture, in Basilicata, is an extinct volcano.
Yes. Its volcanic slopes give Aglianico del Vulture its character.
Look for Aglianico from Campania labelled Irpinia or Taburno. They're often cheaper than Taurasi and show the grape's character well.
What do volcanic soils give Aglianico?
Good drainage and a smoky edge
Volcanic soils drain well and are often linked to smoky, mineral notes.
Aglianico grows mainly in Campania and Basilicata
Volcanic soils drain well and add a smoky edge
Altitude gives cool nights for slow ripening

Taurasi, in Irpinia, Campania, became Southern Italy's first DOCG in 1993. It must be at least 85% Aglianico and age at least three years, one in wood; Riserva needs four years, 18 months in wood. The wines are powerful, tannic and long-lived, with black fruit, tar and earth. Mastroberardino kept the tradition alive after the war.

On Monte Vulture in Basilicata, vineyards sit at 200 to 800 m on volcanic tuff. Aglianico del Vulture is the DOC; Aglianico del Vulture Superiore became DOCG in 2010, with longer ageing. The style is often slightly fresher and more mineral than Taurasi, with the same firm structure.
Match each wine to its region.
Aglianico's great wines come from inland hills.

Both are serious, age-worthy wines. Taurasi is often fuller and more powerful, with more oak influence. Vulture can be leaner and more mineral, with high acidity. Both benefit from 10 years or more in bottle and are best decanted when young.
Taurasi became southern Italy's first ____ in 1993.
Taurasi was the first DOCG of Italy's south.
Taurasi is Campania's DOCG Aglianico, powerful and long-lived
Aglianico del Vulture grows on an extinct volcano
Both need years in bottle and suit decanting

Aglianico's tannin and acidity suit rich, savoury dishes: slow-cooked ragù, braised lamb, roast pork, sausages and hard cheeses like aged pecorino. Its acidity also handles tomato-based sauces. Avoid delicate fish or very sweet sauces.

Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Young Taurasi and Vulture are firm and benefit from decanting for two hours. Good examples age 15 to 25 years, softening into leather, tobacco and dried cherry. Lighter Campania Aglianico is drinkable after two or three years.
Why does Aglianico suit tomato-based sauces?
Its high acidity matches the tomato's acidity
Acidic food needs a wine with at least as much acidity.
Pair a mature Taurasi with a Neapolitan ragù simmered for hours. It's a regional match that's lasted generations.
Young Taurasi is best drunk immediately without decanting.
Not true. Its firm tannins benefit from air and, ideally, years in bottle.
Aglianico suits ragù, lamb and aged pecorino
Decant young wines; the best age 15 to 25 years
It's rare for a southern red to keep such high acidity.
Aglianico's story is volcanic and late-ripening.
Aglianico is grown mainly in northern Italy.
Not true. Its heartland is Campania and Basilicata, in the south.
Hot nights would burn off acidity.
Aglianico is nicknamed the ____ of the south.
For its structure, acidity and ageing potential, like Nebbiolo's Barolo.
Aglianico is tannic, acidic and late-ripening
Campania's Taurasi and Basilicata's Vulture are its great wines
Volcanic soils and altitude shape its style
